==English==

===Alternative forms===
* {{alter|en|learnyng||obsolete}}

===Etymology===
From {{inh|en|enm|lernyng}}, {{m|enm|lernynge}}, from {{inh|en|ang|leornung|t=learning, study}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*liʀnungu|t=learning}}, equivalent to {{suf|en|learn|-ing|id2=gerund noun}}. Cognate with {{cog|osx|lernunga}}, {{cog|de|Lernung}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/ˈlɝnɪŋ/|a=GA}}
* {{IPA|en|/ˈlɜːnɪŋ/|a=RP}}
* {{hyphenation|en|learn|ing}}
* {{audio|en|en-us-learning.ogg|a=US}}
* {{rhymes|en|ɜː(ɹ)nɪŋ|s=2}}

===Noun===
{{en-noun|-|s}}

# {{lb|en|uncountable}} An act in which something is [[learn]]ed.
# {{lb|en|uncountable}} Accumulated [[knowledge]].
#: {{ux|en|The department head was also a scholar of great '''learning'''.}}
# {{lb|en|countable|proscribed}} Something that has been learned.
#* {{RQ:en:New York Times|date=April 5, 2007|author=Stuart Elliott|title=Online Experiment for Print Magazine|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2007/04/05/business/media/05adco.html
|passage=“We’ll take the '''learnings''' and apply them to the rest of our business.”|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20251014084345/https://www.nytimes.com/2007/04/05/business/media/05adco.html|archivedate=14 October 2025}}

It is easily '''earned''' repetition to state that Josephine St. Auban's was a presence not to be concealed.}} #* {{quote-journal|en|date=November 12, 2011|work=BBC Sport |title=[http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/15693231.stm International friendly: England 1-0 Spain] |passage=England will not be catapulted among the favourites for Euro 2012 as a result of this win, but no victory against Spain is '''earned''' easily and it is right they take great heart from their efforts as they now prepare to play Sweden at Wembley on Tuesday.}} # {{lb|en|transitive}} To ==English==
{{wp}}

===Alternative forms===
* {{alter|en|manie||obsolete}}

===Etymology===
From {{inh|en|enm|many}}, {{m|enm|mani}}, {{m|enm|moni}}, from {{inh|en|ang|maniġ}}, {{m|ang|moniġ}}, {{m|ang|maneġ||many}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*manag}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*managaz|t=many; much}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*menegʰ-}}, {{m|ine-pro|*mengʰ-|t=many, sufficient}} or {{inh|en|ine-pro|*méǵh₂s|*méǵh₂-|t=big, great}}.
{{col-top|2|cog}}
Cognate with {{cog|sco|mony|t=many}}, {{cog|yol|many|t=many}}, {{cog|frr|manag}}, {{m|frr|manig}}, {{m|frr|mäning|t=many}}, {{cog|gsw|meng|t=many}}, {{cog|gmw-cfr|mannich}}, {{m|gmw-cfr|männich|t=many}}, {{cog|nl|menig|t=many}}, {{cog|de|manch|t=many, some}}, {{cog|nds|männich}}, {{m|nds-de|männig|t=many}}, {{cog|lb|muench}}, {{m|lb|munch}}, {{m|lb|munnech|t=many}}, {{cog|da|mangen|t=many}}, {{cog|fo|mangur|t=many}}, {{cog|is|margur|t=many}}, {{cog|nb,nn|mang}}, {{m|nn|mange|t=many}}, {{cog|sv|mången|t=many}}, {{cog|got|𐌼𐌰𐌽𐌰𐌲𐍃|t=many; much}}, {{cog|fr|maint|t=many}}; also {{cog|kw|menowgh|t=frequent, often}}, {{cog|ga|minic|t=frequently, often}}, {{cog|gv|mennick|t=frequent, often}}, {{cog|gd|minig|t=frequent}}, {{cog|cy|mynych|t=frequent, often}}, {{cog|be|мно́га|t=many; much}}, {{cog|bg,ru|мно́го|t=many; much}}, {{cog|cs|mnohý|t=many, numerous}}, {{cog|mk|мно́гу|t=very; many; much}}, {{cog|pl|mnogi|t=numerous; plural}}, {{cog|sh|мно̏гӣ}}, {{m|sh|mnȍgī|t=many; much, long; large, numerous}}, {{cog|uk|мно́гий|t=many, multiple}}.
{{col-bottom}}

The noun is from {{inh|en|enm|manye}}, {{m|enm|*menye}}, from {{inh|en|ang|manigeo}}, {{m|ang|menigu|t=company, multitude, host}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*managu}}, {{m|gmw-pro|*managī}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*managō}}, {{m|gem-pro|*managį̄|t=multitude}}, from the same root as the determiner. Cognate with {{cog|gml|menige}}, {{m|gml|menie}}, {{m|gml|menje|t=multitude}}, {{cog|ru|много}}, {{cog|sh|mnogo}}.

===Pronunciation===

* {{a|en|Ireland}} {{homophones|en|mannie|Mannie|manny|Manny}}

===Determiner===
{{head|en|determiner|comparative|more|superlative|most}}

# ''before a countable noun:'' A large, [[indefinite]] number of.
#: {{syn|en|numerous#Determiner}}
#: {{ant|en|a [[couple#English:_small number|couple]] of|a few#Determiner|a [[handful#English:_small number|handful]] of|several#Determiner|;|one#Determiner|;|no#Determiner|zero#Determiner}}
#: {{hyper|en|multiple#Determiner|various#Determiner}}
#: {{hypo|en|countless#Determiner}}
#: {{ux|en|Not '''many''' such people enjoyed playing chess.}}
#: {{ux|en|There are very '''many''' different ways to cook a meal.}}
#: {{ux|en|We spent '''many''' hours and days training, but running clubs boast '''many''' hundreds of faster members.}}
#* {{RQ:KJV|Genesis|17|4|passage=Thou shalt be a father of '''many''' nations.}}
#* {{RQ:Dickens Our Mutual Friend|chapter=15|passage=I did it in a moment of conceit and folly—one of my '''many''' such moments—one of my '''many''' such hours—years.}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-07-06|volume=408|issue=8843|page=68
|title=[http://www.economist.com/news/finance-and-economics/21580518-terrible-name-interesting-trend-rise-smart-beta The rise of smart beta]
|passage=Investors face a quandary. Cash offers a return of virtually zero in '''many''' developed countries; government-bond yields may have risen in recent weeks but they are still unattractive. Equities have suffered two big bear markets since 2000 and are wobbling again. It is hardly surprising that pension funds, insurers and endowments are searching for new sources of return.}}
# ''before a countable noun:'' {{lb|en|in combinations such as 'as many', 'so many', 'this many'}} {{n-g|Used to indicate, demonstrate or compare the number of people or things.}}
#: {{ux|en|We don't need this '''many''' bananas. Put some back.}}
#: {{ux|en|I've never seen these '''many''' stars in the sky.}}
#: {{ux|en|There may be as '''many''' as ten million species of insect.}}
#: {{ux|en|I don't have as '''many''' friends as my sister does.}}

====Usage notes====
* ''Many'' is used only with the plural of countable nouns (except in the combination ''[[many a]]''). Its counterpart used with uncountable nouns is ''[[much]]''. ''Many'' and ''much'' merge in the comparative and superlative forms, which are ''[[more]]'' and ''[[most]]'' for both determiners.

* It was once common to use the indefinite article with ''many'' (''very a many years ago''), as it still is with ''[[few]]'' (''a few good men''). However, this has fallen out of favor except in formations such as "a great/good many."
